questions.subject: english
questions.stem:
次の場面で、相手の発話に対する応答として最も適切なものを選びなさい。
［場面］長い説明を聞いた後、自分の理解が正しいかを確かめたい。
相手：So the bus leaves at nine, but we'll meet at the station first, and then walk to the stop together.
あなた：（　　）

choices.label: ア
choices.text: I have no idea what you mean.

choices.label: イ
choices.text: So, if I understand correctly, we'll meet at the station before nine and walk to the bus stop together?

choices.label: ウ
choices.text: Let me finish what I was saying.

choices.label: エ
choices.text: That's a good question.

questions.explanation: So, if I understand correctly, we'll meet at the station before nine and walk to the bus stop together?　場面の目的と相手との関係に合った表現で応じている。

explanation_detail.approach: まず場面の目的（反対・聞き返し・依頼・断り・提案など）と相手との関係（友人・先生・初対面）を確かめ、その目的を果たす表現を選ぶ。
steps: 場面の目的と相手との関係を確認する。
相手の発話の意図（意見を求める・頼む・誘う）を確認する。
目的に合わない応答、失礼な応答を消す。
答え：So, if I understand correctly, we'll meet at the station before nine and walk to the bus stop together?

stimulus.content:
Today, it seems natural that the clocks in a country all show the same time. But for most of history, each town kept its own time, based on the position of the sun. When the sun was highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the sun reaches its highest point at different moments in different places, a town to the east would be a few minutes ahead of a town to the west.
For centuries, this caused few problems, because people rarely traveled fast enough to notice. The railways changed that. In the nineteenth century, trains could carry passengers between cities in a matter of hours, and having each station use its own local time made timetables confusing and even dangerous. Railway companies began to adopt a single standard time for their lines, and over time, governments followed.
Eventually, the world was divided into time zones, most of them one hour apart, measured from a starting line that passes through Greenwich in London. Within each zone, everyone uses the same clock time, even though it may not match the sun exactly.
The story shows how a new technology can change something as basic as our sense of time. And today, with smartphones that adjust their clocks automatically when we land in a new country, we rarely think about the problem the railways had to solve.

stimulus.content:
Imagine that you have a headache, and a doctor gives you a pill. You take it, and twenty minutes later you feel better. But what if the pill contained no medicine at all, just sugar? Surprisingly, this happens quite often. When people feel better after receiving a treatment that has no active ingredient, we call it the placebo effect.
Why does it happen? One important factor is expectation. If we believe a treatment will help, we may pay less attention to our pain or feel less anxious, and that can change how we feel. Even details like the color of a pill or the confidence of the doctor seem to make a difference in some studies.
The placebo effect is a major reason why new medicines are tested carefully. In a typical trial, one group of patients receives the real drug and another receives a placebo, and usually neither the patients nor the doctors know who is getting which. Only if the real drug works clearly better than the placebo can we say it is effective.
It is important to understand the limits, though. A placebo may help with how we feel, such as pain, tiredness, or nausea, but it cannot shrink a tumor or cure an infection. So the placebo effect reminds us that the mind can influence the body, but it is not a replacement for real medical treatment.

stimulus.content:
Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable forms of communication in the animal world: the honeybee's waggle dance. When a worker bee finds a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run, again and again.
The dance carries two key pieces of information. First, the direction of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. The angle of the run, measured from straight up, matches the angle between the food and the sun. So if the bee runs straight up, the food is in the direction of the sun. Second, the length of the run tells them how far away the food is: the longer she waggles, the farther they need to fly.
What makes this so impressive is that the bees are translating a direction relative to the sun into a direction relative to gravity, in the darkness of the hive. And because the sun moves across the sky during the day, bees seem to adjust their dances to account for this.
Scientists still debate how much the other bees rely on the dance itself and how much on smell. But the waggle dance remains a striking example of how a small insect can communicate abstract information.

So, vertical farming is not going to replace traditional agriculture. But as lighting becomes more efficient and more electricity comes from renewable sources, it may become a valuable way to grow certain crops close to where people live.

stimulus.content:
Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable forms of communication in the animal world: the honeybee's waggle dance. When a worker bee finds a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run, again and again.
The dance carries two key pieces of information. First, the direction of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. The angle of the run, measured from straight up, matches the angle between the food and the sun. So if the bee runs straight up, the food is in the direction of the sun. Second, the length of the run tells them how far away the food is: the longer she waggles, the farther they need to fly.
What makes this so impressive is that the bees are translating a direction relative to the sun into a direction relative to gravity, in the darkness of the hive. And because the sun moves across the sky during the day, bees seem to adjust their dances to account for this.
Scientists still debate how much the other bees rely on the dance itself and how much on smell. But the waggle dance remains a striking example of how a small insect can communicate abstract information.

Today, it seems natural that the clocks in a country all show the same time. But for most of history, each town kept its own time, based on the position of the sun. Because the sun reaches its highest point at different moments in different places, a town to the east would be a few minutes ahead of a town to the west.
For centuries, this caused few problems, because people rarely traveled fast enough to notice. The railways changed that. In the nineteenth century, trains could carry passengers between cities in a matter of hours, and having each station use its own local time made timetables confusing and even dangerous. Railway companies began to adopt a single standard time for their lines, and over time, governments followed.
Eventually, the world was divided into time zones, most of them one hour apart, measured from a starting line that passes through Greenwich in London. Within each zone, everyone uses the same clock time, even though it may not match the sun exactly.
The story shows how a new technology can change something as basic as our sense of time. And today, with smartphones that adjust their clocks automatically when we land in a new country, we rarely think about the problem the railways had to solve.

stimulus.content:
Most of us picture farms as wide fields under an open sky. But in some cities, lettuce and herbs are now being grown indoors, on shelves stacked one above another inside large buildings. This is called vertical farming.
Supporters point to several advantages. Because the plants are grown indoors, crops can be produced all year round, regardless of the weather. Many vertical farms grow plants without soil, feeding the roots with water that contains nutrients, and much of this water is collected and reused, so they can use far less water than traditional farms. And since the farms can be built in cities, food does not have to travel long distances to reach consumers.
However, there is a significant drawback. Sunlight is free, but the LED lights that replace it are not. Lighting, along with heating and cooling, uses a great deal of electricity, which makes vertical farming expensive and, depending on how the electricity is produced, not always better for the environment. Every language borrows words from other languages. English is a good example: a large share of its vocabulary comes from French and Latin, and in recent decades it has also taken words from Japanese, such as tsunami, karaoke, and emoji.

If a language is associated with power, learning, or fashion, speakers may borrow its words even when they already have their own. For centuries after the Norman Conquest, French was the language of the ruling class in England, and many French words entered English through law, government, and cooking.
Borrowed words rarely stay exactly the same. They usually change to fit the sounds and grammar of the new language. Japanese speakers, for instance, add vowels to English words, so that "strike" becomes "sutoraiku." Meanings can change, too. In Japanese, "mansion" usually refers to an ordinary apartment building, not a large, grand house as in English.
Some people worry that borrowing damages a language. But history suggests the opposite: borrowing is one of the ways languages stay alive and keep up with a changing world.

Today, it seems natural that the clocks in a country all show the same time. But for most of history, each town kept its own time, based on the position of the sun. In the nineteenth century, trains could carry passengers between cities in a matter of hours, and having each station use its own local time made timetables confusing and even dangerous. The story shows how a new technology can change something as basic as our sense of time. And today, with smartphones that adjust their clocks automatically when we land in a new country, we rarely think about the problem the railways had to solve.

stimulus.content:
Today, it seems natural that the clocks in a country all show the same time. But for most of history, each town kept its own time, based on the position of the sun. When the sun was highest in the sky, it was noon. For centuries, this caused few problems, because people rarely traveled fast enough to notice. The railways changed that. The story shows how a new technology can change something as basic as our sense of time. And today, with smartphones that adjust their clocks automatically when we land in a new country, we rarely think about the problem the railways had to solve.

stimulus.content:
Every language borrows words from other languages. English is a good example: a large share of its vocabulary comes from French and Latin, and in recent decades it has also taken words from Japanese, such as tsunami, karaoke, and emoji.
Why do languages borrow? The most common reason is need. When people meet a new object, food, or idea, their language may not have a word for it, and the simplest solution is to use the word that comes with it. A second reason is prestige. If a language is associated with power, learning, or fashion, speakers may borrow its words even when they already have their own. For centuries after the Norman Conquest, French was the language of the ruling class in England, and many French words entered English through law, government, and cooking.
Borrowed words rarely stay exactly the same. They usually change to fit the sounds and grammar of the new language. Japanese speakers, for instance, add vowels to English words, so that "strike" becomes "sutoraiku." Meanings can change, too. In Japanese, "mansion" usually refers to an ordinary apartment building, not a large, grand house as in English.
Some people worry that borrowing damages a language. But history suggests the opposite: borrowing is one of the ways languages stay alive and keep up with a changing world.
